newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigeria, China forge stronger ties with accords.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria, China forge stronger ties with accords.

text.p: Nigeria and China signed several cooperation agreements on Monday including one on the vital oil industry, in a move that officials said significantly boosts relations.

Lagos-based diplomats portrayed the boosting of ties as a pragmatic move amid sustained isolation of Nigeria by the West over the military government's failure to embrace democracy, and because of human rights abuses.
Relations between the two nations have grown since military ruler General Sani Abacha seized power in 1993, after a presidential election that would have restored democracy was scuttled by the army.
An official communique said the agreements covered protection of investments, cooperation in electricity and steel projects as well as oil and gas development.
No specific details were released but Nigerian oil minister Dan Etete said on Saturday that China was interested in buying Nigerian crude oil, the West African nation's main export.
Monday's agreements followed a two-day visit to the Nigerian capital by Chinese Prime Minister Li Peng.
Lagos-based diplomats say the boosting of ties with China has been a pragmatic move to forestall Western action against Nigeria at the United Nations Security Council.
"Nigeria needs China to veto any sanctions on the country by the United Nations," said one.

That will however, still leave Western nations able to impose unilateral or regional sanctions as has been done by the United States and the European Union which banned contacts with Nigeria, arms sales and military coopertion, after the election debacle.

Li Peng's visit to Abuja was part of an African tour to thank allies on the continent for helping China defeat a motion of censure against it by the West at last month's U.N. conference on human rights in Geneva.
Ties between Nigeria and China have grown steadily in recent years.
In 1995, Nigeria awarded a $520.6 million contract to China to revamp its dillapidated railways network. The project is scheduled to be completed next year.
Several other lucrative contracts have followed, including the dredging of a major port aimed at opening up the Calabar export processing zone in the southeast.
